newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Nov 19.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Nov 19.

text.p: The stricken Russian Mars space probe is believed to have passed over Southland before crashing into the Pacific Ocean near Easter Island on Monday. A spokeswoman for Prime Minister Jim Bolger said the probe, carrying four small canisters of plutonium, was thought to have passed over Southland at about 100 kilometres height before splashing into the Pacific 3,000 kilometres away at 2.34 p.m. She said New Zealand's ambassador in Washington was alerted by the United States National Security Council just before 2 p.m. when it was realised the probe was likely to pass over New Zealand. Page 1.

NZ First is expected to announce its coalition partner by the end of the month, with sources predicting that National has secured the inside running in the race to power. Now in its fifth week of coalition negotiations, NZ First has apparently reached the final stage of its negotiations with National and Labour and is defining joint policy across a range of issues with its suitors. It is understood the National negotiators have organised a briefing for their caucus for November 28 and backbenchers said they were expecting to see the details of a "macro-agreement" at that time. Page 1.

Speculation continued on Monday on whether National was about to yield to NZ First's demand for a compulsory savings scheme. The scheme, which would see middle-income earners contributing several thousand dollars a year, was slated by many outside the coalition talks as unfair and unworkable. The scheme is believed likely to be opposed by a significant number of National MPs, but several sources in Parliament said they believed many others in National's ranks, including Cabinet ministers, were prepared to accept it. Page 2.

National's promotion-seeking backbenchers may have to rely on a coalition with NZ First to propel them into the front benches. It is understood junior MPs have been actively lobbying Prime Minister Jim Bolger and senior colleagues to get new blood into the Cabinet. Rotorua MP Max Bradford acknowleged on Monday he thought it was time National's senior lineup was "rejuvenated". Page 2.

Falling interest rates were likely to make houses more affordable, ASB Bank economist Rozanna Wozniak says in the bank's December-quater housing report. Wozniak said the outlook for real estate activity was positive, but affordability could be eroded if lower interest rates forced house prices up. She said the Reserve Bank would need time to assess the impact of recent interest rate cuts before allowing further reductions. Page 10.

The high cost of health insurance has been blamed for a significant drop in the number of people covered in the past two years. An industry survey by Sun Alliance says the number of people 15 years and older with medical insurance has dropped three percent to 36 percent compared with a similar survey in 1994. Page 10.

Nationa Mutual Holdings would annouce its first annual result as a listed company in the second week of December, group managing director Geoff Tomlinson said on Monday. Tomlinson would not comment on the likely outcome, but did say the
investment markets were "close" to the key assumptions made in the insurance group's prospectus, with some areas up and others down on the offer document. Page 10.

Lion Nathan has devalued its brands by about $40 million to $2.01 billion. Lion corporate treasurer Jamie Tomlinson said on Monday that about half of the devalutation was due to exchange rates used for the valuations. Page 11.

Wilson and Horton-linked consortium Radio Network would be required to divest some stations as part of its purchase of the Prospect group of stations from Britain's GWP, Commerce Commission chairman Alan Bollard said on Monday. Listed radio company Radio Pacific and Canada's CanWest Global Communications on Monday declared an interest in buying any stations divested as part of the latest deal. Page 11.

New Zealand needs a cheaper dollar to stay competitive in export markets, according to the Irish media magnate and chairman of international food giant Heinz, Tony O'Reilly. "This economy really can only grow through exports...one of the things we have learned as exporters here through Watties is the enormous difficulty of selling New Zealand goods abroad at the 71 cent level," O'Reilly said in Auckland on Monday, citing the vital market of Japan as a particular example. While adding his voice to domestic calls for the dollar to fall, he predicted on Monday that a coalition government would cause the currency to "drop a bit" to more competitive levels.

The management of New Zealand Oil and Gas has cemented virtual control of the prospector by lifting interested party holdings to nearly 50 percent throught what amounted to a share buyback. NZOG chairman Tony Radford said on Monday that the move to buy three percent of the company's shares through its associate Resource Equities was defensive. "There has been a lot of talk and manoeuvres are afoot by some group to engineer a takeover," he said. While not naming the parties involved, he said the share purchases sent a signal to anyone contemplating a move.

Merchant banker Bancorp has put a figure of $23.5 million on the difference between two offers before Power New Zealand's council shareholders in the Thames Valley and Waikato. They have not declared themselves, but the New Zealand Herald understands the Thames-Coromandel, Matamata-Piako, Hauraki and South Waikato district councils have resolved to accept the lower offer from Missouri-based Utilicorp. One reason is that they do not want to be sued by Power NZ like the Waipa District Council, which accepted Mercury's offer.
National Mutual Holdings' full-year result, due next month, would benefit from some net writeback of previous years' capitalised losses, the group managing director Geoff Tomlinson said on Monday.

New Zealand's forestry industry will be increasingly exposed to international commodity cycles because of substantial growth in wood volumes, international ratings agency Standard and Poor's said in a report. The report said that heavy capital expenditure would be required to support the development of additional pulp and paper capacity and other forest product
projects that would use the extra production.
